prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Knowledge is Power. That is what the billboard says and I agree. I am an adult, therefore I understand the threat of passengers. The threat to Our Children, who don't understand the threat of these bird-like, twitchy people. They pose two kinds of threat. To begin with, there is the one we all know about, the preda­tory threat, the hawk-like passengers that prey on children as they sit in front of their computers or televisions. The terrorist threat. That threat is easy to handle. You shoot it. You contain it. You confiscate. You stitch. You bleed from various orifices and sockets, but you survive, you rebuild house and rinse the child. The more serious threat is the diseases passengers carry with them. Internal terrorism. Children love those diseases. It makes them babble like possessed. Their make-up looks like oil in the moonlight. Such children cannot be cleaned off. Kill them. Or turn them into entertainment. Art.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Knowledge, Power, That

outputs.L1:
“Knowledge is power.” So the billboard declares, and I agree.

I am an adult; therefore, I understand the threat posed by passengers—the threat to Our Children, who cannot comprehend the danger presented by these bird-like, twitching people.

They pose two kinds of threat. First, there is the one we all recognize: the predatory threat—the hawk-like passengers who prey on children as they sit before their computers or televisions. The terrorist threat. That threat is straightforward to address. You shoot it. You contain it. You confiscate. You stitch. You bleed from various orifices and sockets, but you survive; you rebuild the house and rinse the child.

The more serious threat is the diseases passengers carry with them: internal terrorism. Children love those diseases. They make them babble as if possessed. Their makeup looks like oil in the moonlight. Such children cannot be cleaned. Kill them—or turn them into entertainment. Art.
outputs.L2:
“Knowledge is Power,” the billboard declares, and I believe it. As a grown person, I recognize the danger posed by passengers. I understand the risk they present to Our Children, who cannot grasp the menace of these jittery, birdlike beings.

They bring two forms of danger. The first is the familiar one: the predatory danger. These hawkish passengers hunt children while they sit before their computers or televisions. It is the terrorist danger. That kind is straightforward to deal with. You shoot it. You restrain it. You seize what must be seized. You sew wounds shut. You bleed from different openings and sockets, but you live through it, repair the home, and wash the child.

The far greater danger is the sicknesses passengers bring inside them. Terrorism from within. Children are drawn to those illnesses. They make them chatter as if possessed. Their cosmetics gleam like oil under moonlight. Children like that cannot be scrubbed clean. Kill them. Or convert them into spectacle. Into art.
outputs.L3:
The narrator strongly endorses the slogan “Knowledge is Power,” presenting it as a guiding principle for survival. In this view, maturity is not simply a matter of age, but of awareness: to be an adult is to understand that danger exists, to recognize its forms, and to respond before it is too late. Childhood is associated with vulnerability and ignorance, while adulthood is defined by suspicion, vigilance, and the ability to identify threats.

A central threat in the passage is represented by the “passengers,” who are described as dangerous outsiders. The imagery used to portray them is bird-like and unnatural, making them seem less than fully human. This dehumanizing description encourages the reader to see them not as ordinary people, but as invasive creatures who endanger children. Their presence is framed as something hostile and contaminating, as though they exist outside the normal boundaries of the community.

The narrator identifies one kind of danger as a direct, predatory, or terrorist threat. This is the kind of threat that can supposedly be met with force. The narrator suggests that such danger can be controlled through violence, containment, and physical separation. In this part of the passage, the solution appears brutally simple: if the enemy can be located and identified, it can be confined, attacked, or destroyed.

However, the narrator presents disease carried by the passengers as a far more serious danger. Unlike an external attacker, disease is invisible, hidden inside the body, and therefore harder to detect or defeat. The narrator describes this as a form of “internal terrorism,” implying that infection works from within and turns the body itself into a site of threat. This makes the danger more frightening because it cannot be easily separated from the innocent children it affects.

The passage becomes especially disturbing in its treatment of infected children. Through violent and dehumanizing imagery, it suggests that once children have been contaminated, they are no longer fully seen as children. They are imagined as impossible to cleanse, as if infection has permanently removed their innocence or humanity. The text even implies that such children may be killed, displayed, or transformed into a form of entertainment or art. This imagery reveals the narrator’s extreme logic: fear of contamination leads not only to the rejection of outsiders, but also to the destruction or objectification of those the narrator claims to protect.
outputs.L4:
The text reads like a paranoid, dystopian warning issued by a society that has come to see “passengers” not as human beings, but as a threat that must be identified, contained, and destroyed. Its language resembles billboard propaganda: blunt, repetitive, and designed to be absorbed instantly by a frightened public. Rather than inviting reflection, it demands suspicion. The figure of the “passenger” is presented as someone who moves among ordinary people while secretly endangering them, especially children. This focus on children intensifies the emotional pressure of the message, turning fear into moral urgency and making violence appear protective rather than cruel.

The imagery is deliberately extreme. The passengers are associated with predation, contamination, and hidden corruption. They are not merely accused of committing harm; they are described as if their very presence is dangerous. The text uses disease metaphors to suggest that they infect the social body from within, spreading weakness, disorder, or moral decay. This makes the threat seem both intimate and invisible. Unlike an enemy who attacks openly, the passenger is imagined as internal, concealed, and already among the innocent. The result is a worldview in which trust becomes impossible and ordinary human contact is recast as a potential source of infection.

This logic is especially disturbing because it transforms victims into monsters. By describing passengers as predators or carriers of corruption, the propaganda strips them of individuality and humanity. They become symbols of danger rather than people with lives, histories, or suffering of their own. Once that dehumanization is complete, extreme responses can be portrayed as necessary. Extermination, exploitation, and violence are reframed as acts of defense, even as acts of care for the community’s children. The language therefore does not simply express fear; it organizes fear into a justification for cruelty.

The conclusion of the text suggests that the most terrifying danger, in this worldview, is not open violence but hidden infection. A visible attacker can be fought, but an internal threat must be rooted out everywhere. This creates a self-perpetuating paranoia: because the danger is imagined as invisible, anyone can be suspected, and any brutality can be excused as prevention. The text ultimately exposes the frightening structure of such propaganda. It shows how a society can convince itself that the vulnerable are dangerous, that compassion is weakness, and that destruction is a form of protection. In doing so, it reveals the moral collapse at the heart of a system that turns fear into permission for extermination.
outputs.L5:
Knowledge is often described as power, and that idea has shaped human history in countless ways. When people gain knowledge, they gain the ability to understand the world, make better decisions, and influence their own future. Knowledge gives individuals the power to solve problems, challenge injustice, and create new opportunities.

That is why education is so important. A society that values knowledge becomes stronger, more innovative, and more independent. People who learn are better prepared to question what they are told, recognize truth, and take meaningful action. In this sense, knowledge is not only personal power but also collective power.

However, power must be used responsibly. Knowledge can help build, heal, and improve lives, but it can also be misused. That is why wisdom, ethics, and compassion must guide the use of knowledge. True power is not simply knowing more than others; it is using what we know to make the world better.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short surreal dystopian monologue from the perspective of a paranoid adult reacting to a billboard that says “Knowledge is Power,” with disturbing propaganda about protecting children from “passengers.”
counterfactuals.output:
The billboard blinks awake at dawn: **KNOWLEDGE IS POWER**.

Under it, a painted mother smiles with all forty of her state-approved teeth while she locks a child inside a glass lunchbox. Around them drift the black silhouettes of **passengers**—hat-brim shadows, elbow-shaped whispers, things with too many hands for holding on.

“Report passengers,” the loudspeaker coos. “Protect the children.”

I pull my collar over my mouth so my thoughts don’t fog the air. Everyone knows passengers can smell memory. They hide in nursery rhymes, in loose baby teeth, in the second spoon at an empty table. Last week, Mrs. Vale’s son drew a door with someone standing behind it, and by evening the Prevention Men had wrapped the whole apartment block in yellow ribbon that screamed when touched.

The billboard turns its huge white eye toward me.

I know things. Too many things. I know my daughter once asked why the moon followed us home. I know I answered. I know answers are how passengers climb in.

So I keep walking, nodding at the mother, the lunchbox, the slogan humming like a toothache in the sky.

Knowledge is power.

Power is safety.

Safety is silence.

And from somewhere inside my coat, very softly, a child’s voice asks if we are there yet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of experimental horror prose in a fragmented, authoritarian voice, mixing public-safety rhetoric, disease panic, terrorism imagery, and the phrase “Knowledge is Power.”
counterfactuals.output:
**NOTICE TO ALL RESIDENTS / NOTICE TO ALL BODIES / NOTICE TO ALL REMAINING LIGHTS**

Remain indoors.

Remain calm.

Remain identifiable.

The Ministry reminds you that panic is a contagion and contagion is a behavior. Cover your mouth when speaking of the dead. Cover your eyes when viewing unauthorized footage. Cover your mirrors after dusk. Symptoms may include fever, trembling, dissent, memory, excessive thirst, and the belief that the sirens are calling your name.

They are not calling your name.

They are calling everyone.

Do not congregate in stairwells, hospitals, underpasses, schools, houses of worship, shopping centers, transit hubs, basements, rooftops, orchards, culverts, or dreams. Crowds provide shelter for infection. Crowds provide shelter for the enemy. Crowds provide shelter for the thing that learned to wear our uniforms.

If you see an unattended package, do not approach it.

If you see an unattended child, do not approach it.

If you see yourself standing unattended at the end of the corridor, do not approach it.

Report all suspicious breathing.

Report all neighbors who have begun to speak in plural.

Report all birds falling upward.

The public-health emergency remains at Level Black. This is not a drill. This has never been a drill. Drills were discontinued after the drills began screaming.

The following materials are prohibited:

1. Unlicensed masks.  
2. Homemade cures.  
3. Maps of the quarantine perimeter.  
4. Photographs of the crater.  
5. Names of the disappeared.  
6. The sound made in the chapel when no one is inside.  
7. Questions.

Citizens are advised that rumors of “conversion” are enemy propaganda. Rumors of “blooming” are enemy propaganda. Rumors that the infected remain conscious during municipal disposal are obscene, corrosive, and punishable by relocation.

Relocation is humane.

Relocation is temporary.

Relocation is never discussed.

The attacks began before the attacks began. First the cough in the broadcast tower. Then the white powder in the envelopes, which was not powder but skin, which was not skin but instruction. Then the commuter train arriving full of wet shoes and no commuters. Then the recorded message transmitted from every emergency phone in the city:

**Knowledge is Power.**

The Ministry denounces this message.

The Ministry repeats this message for your safety.

**Knowledge is Power.**

Do not write it on walls.

Do not carve it into your arms.

Do not teach it to children who wake speaking in radio static.

Citizens must understand: information spreads faster than fever. A fact can be weaponized. A memory can be radicalized. A mouth can become a delivery system. The infected do not bite. They inform. They lean close, with their cracked lips and municipal badges, and tell you what is buried beneath the stadium. They tell you who signed the evacuation order. They tell you why the hospital windows were painted black from the inside.

Then you know.

Then you are dangerous.

Then the cameras turn toward you like flowers.

Mandatory cleansing will begin at 0600. Doors must remain unlocked. Pets must be sealed in approved containers. Grandmothers must be placed near the entrance for ease of assessment. All household gods, heirlooms, medals, urns, tablets, and loose teeth are to be surrendered to uniformed personnel.

Uniformed personnel will not knock.

Uniformed personnel may resemble family members.

Uniformed personnel may weep.

Do not comfort them.

Comfort is contact. Contact is treason. Treason is symptomatic.

In the event of an explosion, assume contamination. In the event of silence, assume explosion. In the event of music beneath the floorboards, lie face down and recite the approved assurances:

I am clean.  
I am loyal.  
I am visible.  
I am not a host.  
I have never dreamed of the red rain.  
I have never opened the blue door.  
I have never heard the children counting backward from the morgue.

Repeat until collected.

Repeat until corrected.

Repeat until the voice repeating is no longer yours.

The Ministry has secured the perimeter. The perimeter has secured the Ministry. Beyond the barricades there is only sickness, fire, doctrine, teeth, and the old city walking on its hands.

Do not look beyond the barricades.

Those who look beyond the barricades report seeing clear skies, functioning hospitals, unmasked faces, and relatives previously declared processed. These hallucinations are common in late-stage exposure. If you experience hope, isolate immediately.

Hope is aerosolized.

Hope survives on surfaces for up to nine days.

Hope has been found in ventilation systems, contraband bread, lullabies, and the soft tissue of the brain.

For your protection, the curfew is now permanent.

For your protection, language will be rationed.

For your protection, the word “why” has been recalled by the manufacturer.

Remain indoors.

Remain calm.

Remain useful.

At 0600, open your doors and lie down with your palms visible.

At 0601, the lights will pass over you.

At 0602, if you still possess unauthorized knowledge, begin praying to the nearest camera.

The camera is listening.

The camera is hungry.

The camera knows your temperature.

**Knowledge is Power.**

Power is quarantine.

Quarantine is love.

Love is obedience.

Obedience is survival.

Survival is not guaranteed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a bizarre satirical speech by an unreliable narrator who believes “bird-like, twitchy people” called passengers are a threat to children, escalating from moral panic into violent absurdity.
counterfactuals.output:
Ladies, gentlemen, and whatever that is in row three wearing a neck pillow in broad daylight—

I rise today not as an expert, because experts are merely people who have been wrong indoors for money, but as a concerned citizen, a parent, and a man who once saw a passenger blink sideways at a child near Gate 14.

Yes, I said it: passengers.

Those bird-like, twitchy people with their rolling little nests, their crinkling snack bags, their haunted eyes scanning departure boards as if receiving instructions from the moon. They shuffle. They perch. They migrate. They form lines for no reason and then complain that the lines are too long. They clutch boarding passes like tiny papery warrants. And we are expected to pretend this is normal.

“For travel,” they say.

Travel! That is how it begins. A suitcase. A ticket. A suspiciously compact banana. Then suddenly our children are asking questions like, “Where is Denver?” and “Why does that man have three hats?” and “Can I have a window seat?” Window seat? A child should be looking out the window at wholesome things: a tree, a mailbox, a neighbor failing to parallel park. Not clouds! Clouds are just sky passengers, and I don’t trust them either.

I have watched these so-called passengers gather around schools, parks, museums, aquariums—places with children, places with benches, places with pretzels. They coo into phones. They flap magazines. They peck at trail mix. They produce tiny bottles of shampoo from nowhere, as if grooming for infiltration.

And what do our officials do? Nothing. They build them terminals. Terminals! A word that literally means “the end.” Wake up.

Our children deserve protection from the passenger lifestyle: the constant announcements, the gate changes, the cultish chanting of “Group B, Group B,” the ritual sacrifice of liquids over 3.4 ounces. I have seen a child exposed to this chaos become, within minutes, “excited for vacation.” Excited! That is how they recruit.

So I propose immediate action.

First, we must install scarecrows in every airport concourse, dressed as stern librarians, to discourage passenger flocking. Second, all rolling suitcases must be fitted with tiny bells so we can hear them skittering in the night. Third, no passenger may approach within fifty feet of a juice box unless accompanied by a responsible non-passenger, such as a dentist, a retired crossing guard, or a large calm dog.

But if they persist—if these twitching migratory snack-goblins continue menacing our youth with postcards, novelty snow globes, and “fun facts about turbulence”—then we must escalate.

I am not calling for violence. I am calling for something far more American: overcomplicated nonsense with a ribbon-cutting ceremony.

We shall construct enormous humane trebuchets outside every terminal, padded with memory foam and scented faintly of cinnamon, and any passenger found loitering with intent to board shall be launched gently into a municipal ball pit until they have reflected on their choices. Repeat offenders will be trapped beneath weighted blankets and forced to listen to calm whale sounds until their pecking instincts subside.

Their snacks will be replaced with confusing soups.

Their neck pillows will be turned against them.

Their luggage carousels will rotate counterclockwise just enough to make them doubt the universe.

And yes, if necessary, we will deploy the pudding cannons.

Some will call this extreme. Some will say, “Sir, you are shouting at a bus station.” To them I say: exactly. The passenger menace is no longer confined to the skies. They have infiltrated trains, ferries, rental cars, and once—God help us—a tandem bicycle.

We must act before every child in this nation is asking to “see the world.” The world? The world is where passengers come from.

Protect the children. Ground the flocks. Ban the tiny pretzels.

And may our great nation never again tremble beneath the soft, rhythmic thunder of sensible walking shoes approaching Gate C9.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, unsettling passage in the style of a fever-dream government warning, where an adult explains why passengers endanger children through predation, terrorism, and infection.
counterfactuals.output:
The announcement begins before the doors close.

It has always been playing, perhaps, beneath the lights and the rubber smell of the aisle, beneath the coughs and ticket chimes and the soft animal shifting of coats. A voice like an adult you almost trust fills the carriage.

**CHILD PASSENGERS ARE REMINDED: ALL STRANGERS ARE VECTORS.**

Your parents may tell you there are ordinary people here. Commuters. Tourists. Grandmothers with bags. Men looking at their phones. Women asleep against the glass.

This is how danger prefers to dress.

A passenger may endanger a child by wanting what should not be wanted. By watching too long. By offering help before help is asked for. By standing between the child and the exit. Such persons may appear clean, polite, credentialed, familiar. They may know the correct words. They may smile in a way that has been practiced in mirrors.

A passenger may endanger a child by carrying belief in a sealed container inside the skull. Belief may detonate without warning. It may be concealed under a winter coat, in a backpack, in silence, in a trembling hand. The public is advised that devotion, grievance, and despair are not visible on inspection.

A passenger may endanger a child by breathing.

The mouth is an unlicensed border. The hands are small governments of contamination. Seats retain histories. Poles remember every palm. A sneeze may travel farther than a promise. Fever may stand beside you holding a paper cup and never introduce itself.

Children are therefore advised not to accept food, touch surfaces, meet eyes, answer questions, follow instructions from non-authorized adults, or assume that the adult beside them remains the same adult from one stop to the next.

Parents and guardians: count the children at departure. Count them at arrival. Count them when the train enters tunnels. Count them when the lights flicker. If the number has changed, do not scream. Screaming assists panic. Panic assists the passenger.

In the event of suspicious kindness, move away.

In the event of unattended luggage, move away.

In the event of coughing, weeping, whispering, praying, staring, bleeding, singing, or excessive stillness, move away.

If there is nowhere to move, lower your head and wait for official darkness.

The voice pauses. The windows show only your reflection, seated among all the other reflections, each one wearing the face of someone who might be innocent.

Then the announcement resumes, softer now, almost tender.

**REMEMBER: THE SYSTEM CANNOT DISTINGUISH BETWEEN A PASSENGER AND A THREAT UNTIL AFTER THE CHILD IS MISSING, INJURED, OR ILL.**

For your safety, fear everyone equally.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a grotesque dystopian propaganda excerpt beginning with “Knowledge is Power,” using repetitive language, paranoia, and surreal imagery about children, passengers, disease, and art.
counterfactuals.output:
“Knowledge is Power,” said the loudspeakers, and the loudspeakers were shaped like children’s mouths, and the mouths were painted red, and the red paint never dried.

Knowledge is Power. Power is Cleanliness. Cleanliness is Obedience. Obedience is Health. Health is the absence of questions.

All passengers must remain seated. All passengers must smile. All passengers must report the passenger beside them, for the passenger beside them may be carrying doubt beneath the tongue, fever behind the eyes, a folded map of forbidden streets in the lining of the coat. The train has no windows because windows encourage distance. The train has no destination because destinations encourage hope.

Children are the lamps of the Nation. Children must be polished. Children must be counted at dawn, counted at noon, counted again when the moon hangs like a surgical mask over the Ministry. If a child dreams in unauthorized colors, notify the nearest Hygiene Officer. If a child draws a bird, ask who taught it to escape. If a child laughs while alone, suspect infection.

Disease begins in the imagination. Disease begins in music. Disease begins in the soft parts of paintings where shadows gather without permission. Citizens are reminded that art is safe only when it praises the wall, the boot, the clock, the Leader’s benevolent eye floating above the factories like a boiled sun.

Knowledge is Power, and Power is watching, and watching is love.

Do not fear the inspectors with mirrors for faces. They are only reflecting your loyalty. Do not fear the nurses who collect whispers in glass jars. They are only preserving public health. Do not fear the children singing under the floorboards. They are only rehearsing the anthem.

Report all stains. Report all silence. Report all passengers who look out through the windowless walls.

The Nation is well. The Nation is clean. The Nation is awake. The Nation has never been sick. The Nation has never cried. The Nation has never painted anything except victory.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
